title: How Noodling Works
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant return from holiday break to discuss noodling (hand fishing), the practice of catching catfish by reaching into underwater nests and letting the male catfish bite the hand, then pulling it out by the gills. They cover its history (first Western mention in 1775 by trader and historian James Adair, Native American roots, Great Depression use), legal status in about thirteen states, the 2008-era documentary Okie Noodling by Bradley Beasley, the dangers (sandpaper-like teeth, drowning, snapping turtles, muskrats, snakes), noodling buddies and spotters, the ethics and environmental debate over removing guarding males, state catch limits during spawning season, the Okie Noodling Tournament in Oklahoma, and noodling in Nigeria. The episode closes with a listener mail item from a skeptical fifteen-year-old questioning whether the show is real.

segments.title: Opening banter and holiday return
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners after a long break, chat about their holidays, and tease the topic of noodling.

segments.title: What noodling is
segments.summary: Noodling, also called hand fishing, hogging, dogging, and stumping, is reaching a hand into an underwater catfish nest so the fish bites and can be pulled out. The hosts compare it to scenes from Flash Gordon and Return of the Jedi.

segments.title: History of noodling and Native American roots
segments.summary: The first Western mention is in 1775 by trader and historian James Adair, who described Native Americans fishing for catfish by hand, sometimes enticing them with red cloth. Other methods included clubbing, spears, bows, and torches. Noodling was used during the Great Depression because it was free.

segments.title: Legality, the documentary, and the tournament origin
segments.summary: Noodling is legal in about thirteen states, up from four about nine years earlier. Bradley Beasley's documentary Okie Noodling helped popularize it, and he started a noodling tournament for the film's ending. Female noodlers such as Rusty McFarland's daughter are mentioned.

segments.title: How the catch works and the male guarding the eggs
segments.summary: Female catfish lay eggs and males guard them, so noodlers catch males. Noodlers wiggle their fingers to attract bites, then work a hand down to the gills and hook them from inside to pull the fish out.

segments.title: Dangers of noodling
segments.summary: Dangers include catfish teeth that feel like sandpaper and can cut the arm, large catfish pulling people under, drowning in submerged roads and currents, and the need for noodling buddies or spotters. Snapping turtles, muskrats, beavers, and snakes can also be encountered. Hosts recommend against noodling alone or as an inexperienced person. Jerry Rider is described as an unusually tough noodler who welcomes snakes.

segments.title: Environmental impact, conservation, and catch limits
segments.summary: Noodlers can indicate waterway health since catfish thrive in murky water. Removing guarding males can expose eggs to predators, raising conservation concerns, though no studies exist. State wildlife departments limit catches during spawning season from May to August, for example three fish per day in Missouri. The hosts discuss the cultural divide between rural noodlers and city anglers.

segments.title: Okie Noodling Tournament and record catches
segments.summary: The Okie Noodling Tournament is held each July at Bob's Pig Shop in Paul's Valley, Oklahoma, with prizes and categories including Fish of the Day, total catch, natural, and scuba noodling. Gaffing and gloves are frowned upon. The 2009 record was a 68.6 pound fish by John Bridges. The Girls Gone Grabbing DVD series is mentioned. Large legendary catfish like General Sherman from The Simpsons are also discussed.

segments.title: Noodling in Nigeria
segments.summary: Noodling is also practiced abroad, including a one-hour contest in Nigeria where the 2008 winner, Yakubu, was arrested for fraud after bringing in a dead fish from another river.

segments.title: Listener mail: accusation of fraud
segments.summary: A fifteen-year-old listener from northern Illinois claims the show is a sham made from edited recordings. The hosts respond and invite him to write back, and mention a sister podcast, Stuff They Don't Want You to Know.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and a reminder to visit the website and iTunes.
